title: Price column on history table view inaccurate
body: The price per unit column on the tabular view of the history is inaccurate. It gives a very false impression of the cost being paid per unit when exported electricity is generated. Since (currently) the app has no idea of the export tariff this is hardly surprising but a quick fix would be to use negative values for the cost of exported electricity. This would overestimate the contribution of exports but would not as currently happens increase the recorded cost of the power. Fixing this properly would require the export tariff information to be taken into account, possible I suppose but needing more work.
author: dqj999

comments.body:
That isn't what that column is for. It's not trying to calculate what you have or haven't paid for electricity at the time. It's simply a list of what the octopus price is for the current tariff, during each 30 minute period. 

The history view only exists so that people can review the actions taken and understand the strategy used to charge the battery - ie why charge/discharge decisions were taken. How much you actually ended up paying is not part of that requirement. I actually only added it as a debugging tool, originally. 

Trying to calculate what you've been billed would need to take account of import/export every minute or so, and would be either very complex or very inaccurate.

This app is only designed to optimise your battery charging schedule. It's not a billing management app, and I'm not interested in building or supporting that - if people want to track their exact costs they can either use the octopus app (with a Home Mini) or use one of the many other apps that focus on this sort of billing accuracy (OctopusWatch, Octopus compare, Home Assistant etc etc).
OK understood.

title: Investigate time-setting not sticking
body: The time returned probably doesn't match the time sent, so should maybe skip for that instance.
author: Webreaper

comments.body: This seems to happen a lot for me - if I'm reading the log file correctly

Yeah, the way the API works is that you can set a value, or read it (like the Control Inverter function). So it's good to check after a write that it succeeded by reading the value back and checking it matches.

But with the clock reset, I think it's like this.

1. Write Time as 02:00:00.00
2. Small delay
3. Read time, comes back as 02:00:00.40
4. I then write again, because the value doesn't match.

But, of course, the time will almost never match because of the tiny gap between reading and writing. So I think this one shouldn't be checked...

Would it be worth adding an acceptable margin of error (5 seconds, 500mS ?) and as long as it returns within that margin accept as having been set successfully ?
Apologies if I'm stating the bleeding obvious :-)
Yeah, that's probably the approach I'll use. But I'll see what works. 😁

title: Further issue with detecting Ohme charging
body: The. Updated Ohme software does not let you avoid dynamic charging now so your car may charge randomly overnight if it is plugged in. I don’t think that any notification is sent when this happens so you could see your house battery being used to charge the car overnight. I can’t think of a way round this with software so I think it will have to raised as a bug/problem with Ohme.
author: dqj999

comments.body: Having thought about this you could use the scheduled action facility to reduce the effect of this. If you set a low power scheduled charge for say the first 4 hours of the cheap period then a high power charge in the last two hours that would correct any clash between the two charging systems and would ensure that the battery was at the desired charge level in the morning, although it might have had a few random charge/discharge cycles.

Yeah, I was going to suggest that if you set a scheduled action to charge the battery all the way through the cheap overnight period (which you'd probably want anyway) then you could prevent the battery discharging to charge the car. Have you seen the latest dev build allows you to specify amps for each scheduled action?

title: Solar PV Forecast Today is much less than the sum of half-hour forecasts
body:
Today the Solar Forecast Today label was predicting 0.8Kw, but the half hour forecast PV figures were predicting about 0.25 kWh every half hour over about 8 slots.  Is the slot forecast meant to be the rate of power generation per hour or the amount of power estimated to be generated in the half hour?

Incidentally it is not clear what the damping factor does to the estimated solar power generation. If 10Kw of solar power was predicted and the damping factor was 25%, would that mean the corrected estimate was 7.5Kw (percentage reduction) or 2.5Kw (multiplier). The damping factor might be counter-intuitive - it basically means "use this percentage of the solcast figures". So if you set 80%, then it'll reduce the solcast estimate by 20%. Again, I can probably make this more intuitive, but I'm re-writing it so it's calculated automatically anyway (see #65) - once that's working, you won't need to manually set the damping factor at all (but I might leave it there as a manual override).

I'm not actually using the solcast data to affect the charging algorithm yet, so until that happens, the oddities in the display aren't critical.

title: Price labelling in Charging Plan
body:
I'm on Octopus Go which has fixed rates (27.10p/unit) from 5:30 to 00:30. I noticed in the Charging Plan that 15:30 to 19:00 was labelled as "Peak" and the rest of time as "Average". 

What causes this difference in the labelling, is it the result of some history of prices?  I know that on Agile these would indeed tend to be Peak charge times.
author: dqj999

comments.body:
Had this question from somebody else so should probably write a faq. 😁

The algorithm assumes the peak time is about 6-8 slots. So it finds the first most expensive set of slots, and marks them as 'peak'. Of course, with Go, the price is constant for hours but all the algo cares about is the next most expensive 6-8 slots.

You'll notice that as time passes, and slots drop off into the past, each 30 minute the peak period will be recalculated - and lo and behold will still be the next 6-8 slots. So the slots marked as peak will move over time until a price trough gets to the front of the slot 'queue'.

I might make an adjustment to make this more intuitive: once the peak period has been found, look for adjoining slots at the same rate or higher than the peak average, and mark them as peak too.

This might also solve #40
This is done in the latest release.

title: Solcast API Calls
body:
I currently have 2 arrays configured in Solcast and use it primarily in a Home Assistant automation and dashboard display. 

I update the dashboard 5 times a day and so that is 10 calls to the API (5 for each array). Since we are limited to 10 API calls per 24 hrs , this means Solis Monitor pinches some of my Home Assistant calls.

I could probably reduce my Home Assistant updates to 3 times per day (6 API calls), so could Solis Monitor survive with 4 calls to the API? It would be up to 4 calls for a single array or 2 calls for twin arrays. 

Would it make sense to parameterise this in the config file?
author: HarryFlatter

comments.body: Okay, next version will have an additional config setting. By default the app will just do one call at 02:13am, but there'll be an option (defaulting to 'off') to have extra calls at 6am and midday, to improve forecasting accuracy, if you have the spare API rate-limit availability.
(Still have to work on the ability to specify multiple solcast API site keys - #52)

Thanks for the update :-).

Since many overnight 'cheap' rates commence at just gone midnight, would it make sense to make that first call at 00:13 so that when you are utilising the forecast data, the app can decide whether or not to action a battery charge based on forecasted solar yield for later that day?

... or parameterise the time of the first call and a yes/no for each of the following 2 calls. That way you can control exactly how many calls will be made (1 or 2 or 3 for single arrays or 2 or 4 or 6 for dual arrays).

Yeah, maybe midnight-ish is better (Solcast gives 97 or so 30-minute forecasts, so that should cover the next day or two). 

I'm reluctant to put too many config options for scheduling etc - it makes the UI more complex and harder to test (we don't want to end up with a UI like the SolisCloud App control screen...). Generally better to be opinionated, and I think midnight as you say will cover the main use-cases.
